Content:
We often use [MATH: z=x+\textrm{i}y] to denote a complex number [MATH: z], where [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are the real and imaginary parts of [MATH: z] respectively.

Content:
We can also depict complex numbers using [MATH: xy]-coordinates. For example, the complex number [MATH: 4+6\textrm{i}] can be represented by the point [MATH: (4,6),] as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e01b84a888874faf1317d370f8f5a6e1]

Content:
In the context of complex numbers, the [MATH: x]-axis is called the real axis, and the [MATH: y]-axis is called the imaginary axis.

Content:
When using a two-dimensional plane to represent complex numbers, we call this the complex plane (another name for it is the Argand diagram). The complex plane is often denoted as [MATH: \mathbb{C}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We often use [MATH: z=x+\textrm{i}y] to denote a complex number [MATH: z], where [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are the real and imaginary parts of [MATH: z] respectively.

Content:
We can also depict complex numbers using [MATH: xy]-coordinates. For example, the complex number [MATH: 4+6\textrm{i}] can be represented by the point [MATH: (4,6),] as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e01b84a888874faf1317d370f8f5a6e1]

Content:
In the context of complex numbers, the [MATH: x]-axis is called the real axis, and the [MATH: y]-axis is called the imaginary axis.

Content:
When using a two-dimensional plane to represent complex numbers, we call this the complex plane (another name for it is the Argand diagram). The complex plane is often denoted as [MATH: \mathbb{C}.]
